title: Statement & Conclusion
summary: Judge what a short statement definitely supports: conclusions (forced or clearly implied by the statement alone), assumptions (what the speaker must take for granted — use the negation test) and courses of action (practical, proportionate responses). The traps are predictable: extreme words, outside facts, overgeneralisation, averages read as limits, and 'only X are eligible' misread as a guarantee.

subtopics.title: Statement and conclusions
subtopics.concept:
A **conclusion** follows only if it is **definitely true on the basis of the statement alone** (plus universal common sense). You are not asked whether it is true in real life — only whether the statement forces it.

A conclusion follows when it:
- restates the statement in other words,
- is a direct, necessary consequence (arithmetic from given data counts), or
- is the obvious intended implication ('may', 'some', 'likely' conclusions often pass).

A conclusion fails when it:
- uses **extreme words** (only, all, always, never, best, must) the statement never used,
- brings in **outside facts** or a cause/effect the statement does not mention,
- **overgeneralises** one case to 'every time' or 'everyone',
- confuses a **necessary** condition with a **sufficient** one ('only those with X are eligible' does not make everyone with X eligible).

tricks.title: Extreme-word filter
tricks.body: Circle words like only, all, always, never, surely, best, entire, must. If the conclusion has one and the statement doesn't, it almost always fails.

example.q:
**Q.** Statement: Regular exercise helps control blood pressure. Conclusion: Exercise is the only way to control blood pressure.

**Sol.** 'Only' is new — the statement says exercise *helps*, not that nothing else works. Does not follow.
example.solution: New extreme word = reject.

tricks.title: Necessary vs sufficient
tricks.body: 'Only X can do Y' means X is required, not that X guarantees Y. Check which direction the conclusion runs.

example.q:
**Q.** Statement: Only graduates can apply for the post. Riya is a graduate. Conclusion: Riya will be selected.

**Sol.** Being a graduate is necessary to apply, not sufficient for selection. Does not follow.
example.solution: 'Only' fixes a gate, not a guarantee.

mistakes: Accepting a conclusion because it is true in real life, though the statement is silent.
Reading 'only those with X' as 'everyone with X'.
Rejecting soft conclusions ('may', 'some') that the statement clearly supports.
Treating an average as a maximum or minimum in data statements.
subtopics.notes:
### What is a statement-conclusion question?
You get a short **statement** (a news line, a rule, a notice, a fact with numbers) and two or three **conclusions**. A conclusion **follows** only if the statement alone makes it definitely true, or makes it the clear, intended meaning. You are not asked whether the conclusion is true in real life. You are asked: *does this statement force it?*

Think of yourself as a strict judge. The statement is the only evidence. Anything the statement does not say is not evidence, even if it is common knowledge.

### When a conclusion follows
1. **Restatement.** It says the same thing in other words. "The library is closed on all Sundays" → "A visitor on a Sunday will find it closed."
2. **Direct consequence.** It follows by simple logic or arithmetic. "360 km in 4.5 hours" → "average speed 80 km/h".
3. **Clear, soft implication.** Words like *some*, *may*, *likely*, *at least one* make a conclusion modest. "A 5% rebate is offered for early payment" → "Some owners are likely to pay early" follows.

### When a conclusion fails
| Trap | What it looks like | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Extreme word | only, all, always, never, best, must, completely | "Exercise is the **only** way to control BP" |
| Overgeneralisation | one case turned into every case | one festival month → "**every year** in festival months" |
| Outside cause | a reason the statement never gave | "sales rose" → "because prices fell" |
| Future guess | what will happen next time | "the metro **will** cut fares again" |
| Average as limit | average read as maximum or minimum | average 80 km/h → "never exceeded 80" |
| Necessary vs sufficient | "only X are eligible" read as "every X gets it" | ten years' service → "she **will** get the award" |

### The "only" and "every" rules
These two words are opposite gates and exams love them.
- **"Only X can get Y"** means X is *necessary*. It tells you who is **out** (the non-X). It does **not** say every X gets Y. Kiran scored 55% and only those with 60% are called → Kiran is not called ✓. Someone with 70% will be selected ✗.
- **"Every X gets Y"** means X is *sufficient*. If Arun is an X, Arun gets Y ✓. But it does not say *only* X get Y.

### Data statements
When the statement has numbers, do the arithmetic. Data conclusions are either forced or contradicted — rarely in between.
- Percentage change: (new − old) ÷ old × 100. ₹40 → ₹50 is 25%; ₹10 → ₹15 is 50%. A bigger rupee rise can be a smaller percentage rise.
- Average × count = total. An average of ₹30,000 for 5 people gives a total of ₹1,50,000, but it does **not** mean each person earns ₹30,000.
- Sales revenue is not profit — cost is unknown unless given.

### Worked example
Statement: The new flyover cut travel time between the station and the bus stand from 40 minutes to 15 minutes.
I. Travel time fell by 25 minutes — arithmetic, **follows**.
II. The flyover was very costly — never mentioned, **fails**.
III. Commuters between the two places now save time — clear implication, **follows**.
Answer: only I and III.

### Quick revision
- Only the statement is evidence. Real-life truth does not matter.
- Follows: restatement, arithmetic consequence, soft clear implication.
- Fails: new extreme word, overgeneralisation, outside cause, future guess, average read as a limit.
- "Only X" = gate (non-X are out). "Every X" = guarantee for each X.
- With numbers, always compute; revenue ≠ profit; average ≠ each value.

patterns.name: Extreme word, overgeneralisation or outside cause
patterns.howToSpot: The conclusion adds only / all / always / every year / because of, or predicts the future, while the statement is about one limited fact.
patterns.logic:
1. Underline the key claim of the statement.
2. Check the conclusion for new extreme words, a wider scope, a new cause or a future prediction.
3. Any such addition means it does not follow; a plain restatement or 'at least one' version does.

*Why it works:* the statement is the only evidence, so anything wider than it is unsupported.

example.q: **Statement:** Metro ridership rose after fares were cut last month. **Conclusion:** The fare cut is the only reason ridership rose.
example.solution: 'Only reason' is a new extreme claim — other causes are not ruled out. **Does not follow.**

patterns.name: Data-based conclusion (compute and compare)
patterns.howToSpot: The statement gives numbers — prices, counts, speeds, averages — and the conclusions state a difference, a percentage or a comparison.
patterns.logic:
1. Compute exactly what the conclusion claims (difference, % change, total = average × count).
2. If it matches, it follows; if it clashes, it fails.
3. Reject claims about quantities not given (profit when only sales are known, maximum when only the average is known).

*Why it works:* arithmetic either forces or contradicts a numeric claim.

example.q: **Statement:** The average monthly salary of 5 employees is ₹30,000. **Conclusions:** I. Total salary is ₹1,50,000. II. Each earns ₹30,000.
example.solution: Total = 5 × 30,000 = ₹1,50,000 → I follows. An average says nothing about each person → II fails. **Only I.**

patterns.name: 'Only X' and 'Every X' rule applied to a person
patterns.howToSpot: A rule with 'only those who…' or 'every … who…', then a named person and a conclusion about that person.
patterns.logic:
1. 'Only X get Y' = X is necessary: non-X are out, but X are not guaranteed Y.
2. 'Every X gets Y' = X is sufficient: any X gets Y.
3. Place the named person against the rule and read off what is certain.

*Why it works:* necessary and sufficient conditions run in opposite directions.

example.q: **Statement:** Only students scoring at least 60% will be called for interview. Kiran scored 55%. **Conclusion:** Kiran will not be called.
example.solution: Kiran is below the gate, so she is out. **Follows.**

patterns.name: Restatement and clear implication (including three conclusions)
patterns.howToSpot: Conclusions that repeat the statement in other words or state its obvious purpose; sometimes three conclusions with pair options.
patterns.logic:
1. Accept a conclusion that says the same thing in different words.
2. Accept a soft, obvious implication (some, likely, can now).
3. For three conclusions, judge each alone, then pick the matching combination.

*Why it works:* a restatement cannot be false if the statement is true.

example.q: **Statement:** The school will stay closed tomorrow due to a heavy-rain warning from the weather department. **Conclusions:** I. Students need not come to school tomorrow. II. The weather department has warned of heavy rain.
example.solution: Both repeat parts of the statement. **Both follow.**

subtopics.title: Statement and assumptions
subtopics.concept:
An **assumption** is an unstated belief the speaker **must** hold for the statement (advice, appeal, notice, advertisement) to make sense. It is taken for granted *before* the statement is made.

**Negation test**: negate the assumption. If the statement then becomes pointless or self-defeating, the assumption is implicit. Example: 'Book your tickets early to avoid the rush' assumes there will be a rush — negate it ('there will be no rush') and the advice is pointless.

Assumptions are usually modest (some people, likely effect). A claimed assumption that the action will produce a **total** result (accidents will stop completely) is not needed and is not implicit.

tricks.title: Negation test
tricks.body: Put 'not' in the assumption. Does the speaker still have a reason to say what they said? If not, the assumption is implicit.

example.q:
**Q.** Notice: 'Use the stairs during the lift maintenance on Tuesday.' Assumption: The building has stairs usable by residents.

**Sol.** Negate: 'there are no usable stairs' — the notice becomes absurd. Implicit.
example.solution: If negation kills the statement's purpose, the assumption is implicit.

mistakes: Choosing assumptions that are desirable but not required.
Accepting 100%-effect assumptions (will stop completely, everyone will obey).
Confusing an assumption (before the statement) with a conclusion (after it).
subtopics.notes:
### What is an assumption?
An **assumption** is an idea the speaker takes for granted *before* speaking. It is not written in the statement, but without it the statement would make no sense. When a mother says "Take your umbrella, it will rain", she assumes the umbrella will be useful and that you are going out. She never says so — she does not need to.

A conclusion comes *after* a statement (what follows from it). An assumption comes *before* it (what the speaker already believes). Keep these two apart.

### The negation test
This single test solves almost every question.
1. Take the assumption and put **not** into it.
2. Read the statement again with the negated idea in mind.
3. If the statement now becomes **pointless, foolish or self-defeating**, the assumption is **implicit**. If the statement still makes sense, the assumption is **not** implicit.

Example: Notice — "Use the stairs on Tuesday; the lift will be under repair." Assumption: the building has usable stairs. Negate it: "there are no usable stairs". Now the notice is absurd → implicit.

### Where assumptions come from
| Statement type | What it usually assumes |
|---|---|
| Advice ("Do X") | X is possible for the listener, and X will help |
| Appeal / request | the listener can and may respond |
| Notice | the readers will read it and can follow it |
| Advertisement | some buyers want what the hook offers |
| Decision / policy | the plan is feasible and will have *some* good effect |

### Assumptions that are NOT implicit
- **Total-effect claims.** "CCTV will completely stop signal jumping" — the authority only needs to expect *some* improvement. A 100% result is never required.
- **Comparisons with rivals.** An advert for a purifier need not assume it is the cheapest or the best; it only assumes people want safe water.
- **Contradictions.** An assumption that clashes with the statement ("tank cleaning will take a week" when the notice says 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.) cannot be implicit.
- **Extreme words.** "Nobody can...", "all people...", "only this method..." are rarely needed.
- **Things that would make the statement unnecessary.** "All riders already wear helmets" — if true, the helmet poster would be pointless, so the poster cannot assume it.

### Worked examples
1. Scheme: free cycles for girl students of Class IX to improve attendance. I. Some girls find it hard to reach school — negate: "none find it hard" → the scheme is pointless → **implicit**. II. Every girl will now attend daily — total effect → **not implicit**. Answer: only I.
2. The railway will add two coaches to a train during the festival season. I. More people are likely to travel then — negate: "no more people" → extra coaches pointless → **implicit**. II. The train can run with two extra coaches — negate: "it cannot" → the decision is impossible → **implicit**. Answer: both.

### Quick revision
- Assumption = unstated belief the statement depends on; it comes before the statement.
- Negation test: negate it; if the statement collapses, it is implicit.
- Advice and decisions assume feasibility and some benefit — both usually implicit.
- Reject total effects, rival comparisons, contradictions and extreme words.
- An assumption that would make the statement unnecessary is never implicit.

patterns.name: Advice or request — the negation test
patterns.howToSpot: Someone advises or requests: 'Do X', 'Please do X', 'Carry X'.
patterns.logic:
1. Negate each assumption.
2. If the advice becomes pointless (it would not help, or the listener cannot follow it), the assumption is implicit.
3. If the advice still makes sense, or the assumption contradicts it, it is not implicit.

*Why it works:* advice only makes sense if it is possible and useful.

example.q: **Statement:** 'Wear a helmet while riding,' says a traffic poster. **Assumption:** A helmet can reduce head injuries.
example.solution: Negate: helmets do not reduce injuries → the poster is pointless. **Implicit.**

patterns.name: Advertisement or notice
patterns.howToSpot: An advert with a hook (price, speed, convenience) or a notice asking readers to do something.
patterns.logic:
1. An advert assumes some buyers value its hook — implicit.
2. It does not assume it beats every rival — not implicit.
3. A notice assumes readers can act on it; anything contradicting the notice's own details is not implicit.

*Why it works:* the advert or notice would be useless without its audience responding.

example.q: **Advertisement:** 'Weekend yoga classes for busy office-goers.' **Assumptions:** I. Some office-goers are free on weekends. II. Office-goers cannot do yoga on weekdays.
example.solution: Negate I → nobody could attend → implicit. II is an extreme 'cannot' the advert does not need. **Only I.**

patterns.name: Total-effect or extreme assumption (trap)
patterns.howToSpot: One assumption says the step will work completely, for everyone, always.
patterns.logic:
1. Spot the total words: completely, every, all, never again.
2. A decision-maker needs only some benefit, so the total claim is not implicit.
3. The modest partner ('some people may…') usually is implicit.

*Why it works:* nobody plans only for perfect outcomes; partial benefit is enough reason to act.

example.q: **Statement:** CCTV cameras will be installed at junctions to reduce signal jumping. **Assumption:** CCTV will completely stop signal jumping.
example.solution: Only some reduction is needed for the decision to make sense. **Not implicit.**

patterns.name: Decision or policy — feasibility and purpose
patterns.howToSpot: A government body or company announces a plan: add coaches, open a branch, launch a scheme.
patterns.logic:
1. The plan assumes a need exists (customers, travellers, a problem to solve).
2. It assumes the plan can actually be carried out.
3. It does not assume unrelated extra steps (closing other branches) or total success.

*Why it works:* a sensible authority acts only when there is a need and the step is possible.

example.q: **Statement:** A company will open a branch in Pune to serve its growing customers there. **Assumption:** The company has customers in Pune.
example.solution: Negate: no customers in Pune → the branch has no purpose. **Implicit.**

subtopics.title: Courses of action
subtopics.concept:
The statement describes a problem or situation; a **course of action** follows if it is a **practical, proportionate step** that addresses the problem (solves, reduces, or investigates it) and is within reach of the proper authority.

Reject actions that are:
- **extreme or disproportionate** (ban, shut down permanently, punish everyone),
- **unrelated** to the stated problem, or
- **impractical** (require the impossible, e.g. stop the monsoon).

Two actions can both follow — a long-term fix (repair roads) and a short-term relief (deploy traffic police) are independent and often both valid.

tricks.title: Proportion check
tricks.body: Ask: would a sensible administrator actually do this tomorrow? Investigating, repairing, warning, supplying, treating usually pass; banning, shutting forever, blaming everyone fail.

example.q:
**Q.** Statement: A few buses of a city route broke down this week. Action: Scrap the entire bus fleet.

**Sol.** Disproportionate — a few breakdowns call for inspection and repair, not scrapping all buses. Does not follow.
example.solution: Fix the problem, don't nuke the system.

mistakes: Accepting harsh blanket bans as 'strong action'.
Rejecting a valid short-term relief because it is not a permanent solution.
Choosing actions that address a different problem than the one stated.
subtopics.notes:
### What is a course of action?
The statement describes a **problem** or a situation. Each course of action is a proposed step. A course of action **follows** if a sensible authority would take it: it is **practical**, **proportionate** to the problem, and **related** to it. It should solve the problem, reduce its harm, or find out its cause.

Think of yourself as a calm, fair district officer. You do not panic, you do not punish everyone for one person's fault, and you do not ignore the problem.

### The three filters
1. **Relevance.** Does the action touch the stated problem? Poor maths results → appoint a maths teacher ✓; widen the village road ✗.
2. **Practicality.** Can it actually be done, by the proper authority, in reasonable time? Shifting a whole city's population because of a water shortage ✗.
3. **Proportion.** Is the response sized to the problem? A few students copying → act against those students and tighten invigilation ✓; cancel every student's result ✗.

### Actions that usually follow
- **Investigate**: inquiry, testing, inspection, tracing the culprits.
- **Repair or fix**: mend streetlights, correct display boards, improve drainage.
- **Relief**: rescue stranded families, send water tankers, keep hospital beds ready.
- **Awareness and regulation**: warn, advise, ration, regulate traffic until safety is checked.
- **Action as per rules** against those actually responsible.

### Actions that usually fail
- **Blanket bans**: ban all private buses because one operator overcharged.
- **Permanent shutdowns** for a one-time or local problem.
- **Punishing everyone** for the fault of a few.
- **Unrelated actions** that address a different problem.
- **Impossible or absurd steps**: stop the monsoon, never go out after dark.

### Two actions can both follow
Problems often need a **short-term relief** and a **long-term fix**. Flooded low-lying areas: send rescue teams now (relief) *and* improve drainage for the future (fix). Neither cancels the other. Do not reject a relief step because it is not permanent, and do not reject a long-term fix because it is not immediate.

### Investigate before punishing
When the cause is not yet known (a bridge cracks after two years), an **inquiry** followed by action against those found responsible is proportionate. Punishing a named person without an inquiry, or banning all bridges, is not.

### Worked example
Statement: The reservoir supplying a city has fallen to a very low level after poor rainfall.
I. Ration water and urge residents to save it — practical, related → **follows**.
II. Send tankers to areas with acute shortage — relief → **follows**.
III. Shift the population to another city — absurd and impractical → **fails**.
Answer: only I and II.

### Quick revision
- Follows = practical + proportionate + related to the stated problem.
- Good verbs: investigate, repair, relieve, regulate, warn, act as per rules.
- Bad verbs: ban all, shut forever, punish everyone, do something unrelated or impossible.
- Short-term relief and long-term fix can both follow.
- Unknown cause → inquiry first, then action against those responsible.

patterns.name: Practical fix vs blanket ban
patterns.howToSpot: One action repairs, traces or regulates the problem; the other bans, withdraws or stops something for everyone.
patterns.logic:
1. Ask whether the action targets the actual cause.
2. Keep repairs, inquiries and action as per rules.
3. Reject bans that punish the many for a local problem.

*Why it works:* a sensible authority fixes the fault, not the whole system.

example.q: **Statement:** Fake ₹500 notes are circulating in a district. **Actions:** I. Trace the gang printing them. II. Withdraw all ₹500 notes in the country.
example.solution: I targets the cause. II is a nationwide overreaction to a district problem. **Only I.**

patterns.name: Short-term relief plus long-term fix
patterns.howToSpot: A disaster or crisis, with one action giving immediate relief and another preventing a repeat (sometimes a third absurd action).
patterns.logic:
1. Relief steps (rescue, tankers, extra beds) follow.
2. Preventive steps (drainage, cleaning breeding sites) also follow.
3. Reject only the absurd or extreme third option.

*Why it works:* relief and prevention solve different parts of the same problem.

example.q: **Statement:** Low-lying areas are flooded and families are stranded. **Actions:** I. Send rescue teams. II. Improve drainage in these areas.
example.solution: Relief now and prevention later are both sensible. **Both follow.**

patterns.name: Unrelated action
patterns.howToSpot: One action sounds useful in general but does not touch the problem stated.
patterns.logic:
1. Name the problem in three words (poor maths results, wrong platform display).
2. Keep actions that address those words.
3. Reject anything aimed at a different issue, however good it sounds.

*Why it works:* a course of action must follow from THIS statement, not from general wishes.

example.q: **Statement:** Passengers miss trains because display boards show wrong platforms. **Actions:** I. Check and correct the display system. II. Reduce ticket prices.
example.solution: Only I touches the display problem. **Only I.**

patterns.name: Punish all vs act against those responsible
patterns.howToSpot: Wrongdoing by a few (copying, poor construction) with one action punishing everyone and another investigating or acting against the guilty.
patterns.logic:
1. Keep action against those actually responsible, as per rules.
2. Keep an inquiry when the cause is not yet known.
3. Reject collective punishment of the innocent.

*Why it works:* proportion means the response is aimed at the wrongdoers only.

example.q: **Statement:** A few students were caught copying. **Actions:** I. Cancel results of all students. II. Act against those caught and tighten invigilation.
example.solution: I punishes the innocent. II is proportionate. **Only II.**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A notice, news line or fact followed by two conclusions I and II.
pyqPatterns.approach: Judge each conclusion only against the statement. Reject new extreme words, wider scope, outside causes and future guesses. Keep restatements and clear, soft implications.

example.q: **Statement:** Sales of phones rose sharply in October this year. **Conclusions:** I. Every year phone sales rise in festival months. II. Phone prices were cut in October.
example.solution: I overgeneralises one year; II adds an unstated cause. **Neither follows.**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The statement carries numbers — prices, marks, distances, averages.
pyqPatterns.approach: Do the arithmetic the conclusion claims. Percentages are on the old value; average × count = total; an average never fixes a maximum; sales are not profit.

example.q: **Statement:** A notebook rose from ₹40 to ₹50 and a pen from ₹10 to ₹15. **Conclusion:** The notebook price rose by a larger percentage.
example.solution: Notebook 25%, pen 50% → **does not follow.**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Only those who…' or 'every… who…' with a named person.
pyqPatterns.approach: 'Only X' is a gate: non-X are out, X are not guaranteed. 'Every X' is a guarantee: each X gets it. Read the person against the correct direction.

example.q: **Statement:** Only employees with ten years' service are eligible for an award. Rekha has twelve years. **Conclusion:** Rekha will receive the award.
example.solution: Ten years is necessary, not sufficient → **does not follow.**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Three conclusions; options list pairs or all three.
pyqPatterns.approach: Judge each conclusion separately, write ✓ or ✗ beside it, then match the pattern of ticks to the options.

example.q: **Statement:** A flyover cut travel time from 40 to 15 minutes. I. Time fell by 25 minutes. II. The flyover was costly. III. Commuters save time.
example.solution: I ✓ (arithmetic), II ✗ (not mentioned), III ✓ → **only I and III.**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Advice, notice, advertisement or decision with two assumptions.
pyqPatterns.approach: Use the negation test: negate the assumption; if the statement becomes pointless, it is implicit. Reject total effects, rival comparisons and contradictions.

example.q: **Statement:** 'Book tickets early to avoid the rush.' **Assumption:** There is likely to be a rush.
example.solution: Negate: no rush → the advice is pointless → **implicit.**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A government or company decision followed by assumptions about need and feasibility.
pyqPatterns.approach: A decision assumes a need exists and that the step can be carried out. It does not assume total success or unrelated extra steps.

example.q: **Statement:** Two extra coaches will be added to a train in the festival season. **Assumption:** The train can run with two extra coaches.
example.solution: Negate: it cannot → the decision is impossible → **implicit.**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A problem is described; two or three proposed actions.
pyqPatterns.approach: Keep practical, proportionate and related steps — investigate, repair, relieve, regulate, act as per rules. Reject bans, permanent shutdowns, collective punishment and unrelated steps.

example.q: **Statement:** Several hostel students fell ill after dinner. **Actions:** I. Test the food and inspect the kitchen. II. Shut the hostel permanently.
example.solution: I is proportionate; II is an overreaction → **only I.**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A crisis with one immediate-relief action and one long-term preventive action.
pyqPatterns.approach: Both types are valid and do not cancel each other. Reject only the third, absurd option if there is one.

example.q: **Statement:** Dengue cases have risen sharply. **Actions:** I. Fogging and removal of stagnant water. II. Hospitals keep extra beds ready.
example.solution: Prevention and relief → **both follow.**

solvedExamples.q:
**Statement:** The municipal corporation has announced a 5% rebate on property tax paid on or before 30 June.

**Conclusions:**
I. Some property owners are likely to pay their tax on or before 30 June.
II. A penalty will be charged on property tax paid after 30 June.

Which of the conclusions follow(s) from the statement?
solvedExamples.solution: I: A rebate is offered precisely to encourage early payment; that some owners will respond is the clear implication — **follows**. II: The statement says nothing about a penalty; missing a rebate is not the same as paying a fine — outside information, **does not follow**. Answer: **Only I**.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Rebate ≠ penalty: reject anything the statement never mentioned.

solvedExamples.q:
**Statement:** In a school, 240 of the 400 students in Class XI chose the Science stream and all the others chose Commerce.

**Conclusions:**
I. 60% of the Class XI students chose Science.
II. More Class XI students chose Commerce than Science.

Which of the conclusions follow(s) from the statement?
solvedExamples.solution: I: 240 ÷ 400 = 0.6 = 60% — **follows**. II: Commerce = 400 − 240 = 160, which is less than 240 — the statement contradicts it, **does not follow**. Answer: **Only I**.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Do the arithmetic; data conclusions are either forced or contradicted.

solvedExamples.q:
**Statement:** A mother tells her son, 'Carry your umbrella — the forecast says there will be heavy rain this evening.'

**Assumptions:**
I. The weather forecast is generally reliable.
II. The son will be outdoors this evening.

Which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement?
options: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
solvedExamples.solution: Negate I: 'the forecast is unreliable' — then advising an umbrella on its basis makes no sense, so I is **implicit**. Negate II: 'the son will stay indoors' — the umbrella advice becomes pointless, so II is **implicit**. Answer: **Both**.

solvedExamples.q:
**Statement:** Several students of a college hostel fell ill after eating dinner from the hostel mess.

**Courses of action:**
I. The mess food and drinking water should be tested and the kitchen inspected.
II. The hostel should be shut down permanently.

Which of the courses of action logically follow(s)?
options: Only course of action I follows
Only course of action II follows
solvedExamples.solution: I is a practical, proportionate step to find and remove the cause — **follows**. II is a drastic overreaction to a single incident and does not address the cause — **does not follow**. Answer: **Only I**.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Investigate and fix = yes; shut down forever = no.

practice.q:
**Statement:** All candidates must carry an original photo identity card to the examination hall; candidates without one will not be allowed to enter.

**Conclusions:**
I. A candidate without an original photo identity card will not be allowed into the hall.
II. The photo identity card is the only document a candidate needs to carry.

Which of the conclusions follow(s) from the statement?
practice.solution: I simply restates the rule — **follows**. II adds 'only': the statement never says no other document (such as the admit card) is required — **does not follow**. Answer: **Only I**.
practice.shortcut: Restatement passes; a new 'only' fails.

practice.q:
**Statement:** Sales of mobile phones in the city rose sharply during the festival month of October this year.

**Conclusions:**
I. Every year, people in the city buy more phones in festival months than in other months.
II. Mobile phone prices were reduced in October.

Which of the conclusions follow(s) from the statement?
practice.solution: I stretches one year's data to 'every year' — overgeneralisation, **does not follow**. II supplies a cause (price cut) the statement never mentions — outside information, **does not follow**. Answer: **Neither**.
practice.shortcut: One observation ≠ a rule; an unstated cause ≠ a conclusion.

practice.q:
**Statement:** A train covered a distance of 360 km in 4 hours 30 minutes.

**Conclusions:**
I. The average speed of the train was 80 km/h.
II. The speed of the train never exceeded 80 km/h.

Which of the conclusions follow(s) from the statement?
practice.solution: I: 360 ÷ 4.5 = 80 km/h — **follows**. II: an average says nothing about the maximum; the train could have run faster on some stretches and slower on others — **does not follow**. Answer: **Only I**.
practice.shortcut: Average speed fixes the average, never the top speed.

practice.q:
**Statement:** Only employees who have completed ten years of service are eligible for the long-service award. Rekha has completed twelve years of service.

**Conclusions:**
I. Rekha is eligible for the long-service award.
II. Rekha will receive the long-service award.

Which of the conclusions follow(s) from the statement?
practice.solution: 'Only those with ten years are eligible' makes ten years **necessary**, not **sufficient**: it tells us who is *excluded* (under ten years), not that everyone above ten years is eligible — there may be other conditions. So I does **not** definitely follow, and II (actually receiving it) is even further away. Answer: **Neither**.
practice.shortcut: 'Only X are eligible' → not-X are out; it never says X are in.

practice.q:
**Statement:** Every employee of the firm who works on a Sunday gets a compensatory day off. Arun, an employee of the firm, worked last Sunday.

**Conclusions:**
I. Arun is entitled to a compensatory day off.
II. Arun works on every Sunday.

Which of the conclusions follow(s) from the statement?
practice.solution: The rule is universal ('every employee who works on a Sunday'), and Arun satisfies it, so I **follows**. II turns one Sunday into every Sunday — **does not follow**. Answer: **Only I**.
practice.shortcut: 'Every X gets Y' + Arun is X → Arun gets Y. Contrast with the 'only' trap.

practice.q:
**Statement:** The price of a notebook rose from ₹40 to ₹50, while the price of a pen rose from ₹10 to ₹15.

**Conclusions:**
I. The price of the notebook rose by a larger percentage than the price of the pen.
II. The price of the pen rose by 50%.

Which of the conclusions follow(s) from the statement?
practice.solution: Notebook: (50 − 40)/40 = 25%. Pen: (15 − 10)/10 = 50%. I claims 25% > 50% — false, **does not follow** (a bigger rupee rise is not a bigger percentage rise). II is exactly 50% — **follows**. Answer: **Only II**.
practice.shortcut: Compare percentages on the base, not the rupee jump.

practice.q:
**Statement:** Doctors advise that adults should sleep for at least seven hours a night to stay healthy.

**Conclusions:**
I. Sleeping for more than seven hours a night is harmful for adults.
II. Regularly sleeping for less than seven hours may affect an adult's health.

Which of the conclusions follow(s) from the statement?
practice.solution: I invents a harm from sleeping more — the advice sets a minimum, not a maximum — **does not follow**. II is the direct implication of 'at least seven hours to stay healthy' and is suitably soft ('may') — **follows**. Answer: **Only II**.
practice.shortcut: 'At least' sets a floor; it says nothing about going above it.

practice.q:
**Statement:** The city library will remain closed on all Sundays and on all public holidays.

**Conclusions:**
I. The library will be closed on Republic Day, a public holiday.
II. A reader who visits the library on a Sunday will find it closed.

Which of the conclusions follow(s) from the statement?
practice.solution: I: Republic Day is a public holiday, and the library is closed on all public holidays — **follows**. II: it is closed on all Sundays — **follows**. Answer: **Both**.
practice.shortcut: 'All Sundays and all public holidays' covers both specific cases.

practice.q:
**Statement:** In a class of 50 students, 30 passed in Mathematics and 35 passed in Science. Every student passed in at least one of the two subjects.

**Conclusions:**
I. 15 students passed in both subjects.
II. 20 students passed only in Science.

Which of the conclusions follow(s) from the statement?
practice.solution: Both = 30 + 35 − 50 = 15, so I **follows**. Only Science = 35 − 15 = 20, so II **follows**. Answer: **Both**.
practice.shortcut: n(A∩B) = n(A) + n(B) − total when nobody fails both.

practice.q:
**Statement:** All the seats for the evening show of the play were sold out two days before the show.

**Conclusions:**
I. There was high demand for tickets to the evening show.
II. The morning show of the play was also sold out.
III. At least some tickets for the evening show were sold before the day of the show.

Which of the conclusions follow from the statement?
options: All of I, II and III follow
practice.solution: I: selling out two days early clearly indicates high demand — **follows**. II: nothing is said about the morning show — **does not follow**. III: all seats were gone two days before, so tickets were certainly sold before the show day — **follows**. Answer: **Only I and III**.
practice.shortcut: Judge each conclusion alone, then find the matching pair.

practice.q:
**Statement:** Advertisement: 'Learn to swim in just 15 days — join our summer swimming camp!'

**Assumptions:**
I. Some people want to learn swimming in a short time.
II. Nobody can learn swimming in less than 15 days.

Which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement?
options: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
practice.solution: I: the '15 days' pitch only attracts customers if people value quick learning — negate it and the advert loses its point, so I is **implicit**. II: the camp need not believe faster learning is impossible; it only claims 15 days is enough — **not implicit**. Answer: **Only I**.
practice.shortcut: An advert assumes its hook appeals to someone; it assumes nothing about rivals.

practice.q:
**Statement:** The state transport department has decided to put up road-safety hoardings along the national highway.

**Assumptions:**
I. Road accidents on the highway will stop completely once the hoardings are put up.
II. At least some drivers will read the hoardings and may drive more carefully.

Which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement?
options: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
practice.solution: I demands a 100% effect — the department only needs to expect *some* benefit, so I is **not implicit**. II: negate it ('no driver will read them') and the decision becomes pointless, so II is **implicit**. Answer: **Only II**.
practice.shortcut: Reject total-effect assumptions; keep the modest one the plan depends on.

practice.q:
**Statement:** The class teacher said, 'Please submit your filled forms by Friday so that I can send the list to the office on Monday.'

**Assumptions:**
I. The students are in a position to submit the forms by Friday.
II. The list to be sent to the office depends on the students' forms.

Which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement?
options: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
practice.solution: Negate I: 'students cannot submit by Friday' — the request is pointless, so I is **implicit**. Negate II: 'the list does not need the forms' — then linking the deadline to Monday's list makes no sense, so II is **implicit**. Answer: **Both**.
practice.shortcut: Both halves of the teacher's sentence rest on one assumption each.

practice.q:
**Statement:** After the monsoon, a large number of potholes have appeared on the city's main road, causing long traffic jams every day.

**Conclusions:**
I. The municipal body should repair the potholes as early as possible.
II. All vehicles should be banned from the main road until the next monsoon.
III. Traffic police should be deployed on the road to manage the jams until the repairs are completed.

Which of the conclusions follow from the statement?
options: All of I, II and III follow
practice.solution: I fixes the root cause — **follows**. II is a disproportionate ban that paralyses the city and does not repair anything — **does not follow**. III is a sensible short-term relief while repairs go on — **follows**. Answer: **Only I and III**.
practice.shortcut: A permanent fix and a temporary relief can both be valid.

practice.q:
**Statement:** Farmers in a district report that a new type of pest has been damaging their standing crops.

**Courses of action:**
I. The farmers should be told to stop cultivation in the district.
II. Agricultural experts should be sent to identify the pest and advise the farmers on control measures.

Which of the courses of action logically follow(s)?
options: Only course of action I follows
Only course of action II follows
practice.solution: I is drastic and destroys the farmers' livelihood instead of tackling the pest — **does not follow**. II is a practical step that addresses the actual problem — **follows**. Answer: **Only II**.
practice.shortcut: Tackle the pest, not the farming.

practice.q:
**Statement:** Ravi scored the highest marks in Class X of his school this year.

**Conclusions:**
I. Ravi is the most intelligent student of the school.
II. No other Class X student of his school scored more than Ravi this year.

Which of the conclusions follow(s) from the statement?
practice.solution: I turns one exam result into a claim about intelligence across the whole school — a new, wider claim, so it **does not follow**. II simply restates 'highest marks' — **follows**. Answer: **only II**.
practice.shortcut: Marks in one exam ≠ 'most intelligent'. Restatement follows.

practice.q:
**Statement:** After a new bus route was started, the number of students reaching the village school late fell.

**Conclusions:**
I. The new bus route is the only reason fewer students now come late.
II. The bus route will be extended to other villages next year.

Which of the conclusions follow(s) from the statement?
practice.solution: I adds the extreme word 'only'; other causes are not ruled out — **does not follow**. II predicts a future plan that the statement never mentions — **does not follow**. Answer: **neither**.
practice.shortcut: 'Only reason' and future plans are both outside the statement.

practice.q:
**Statement:** A shop sold 120 shirts in January and 150 shirts in February.

**Conclusions:**
I. The number of shirts sold rose by 25% from January to February.
II. The shop made more profit in February than in January.

Which of the conclusions follow(s) from the statement?
practice.solution: I: rise = (150 − 120) ÷ 120 × 100 = 25% — **follows**. II: profit depends on prices and costs, which are not given; more pieces sold does not prove more profit — **does not follow**. Answer: **only I**.
practice.shortcut: Percentage change is on the old value. Sales ≠ profit.

practice.q:
**Statement:** The average weight of 4 boxes is 15 kg. When a fifth box is added, the average of the 5 boxes becomes 16 kg.

**Conclusions:**
I. The fifth box weighs 20 kg.
II. The fifth box is heavier than each of the first four boxes.

Which of the conclusions follow(s) from the statement?
practice.solution: I: total of 5 boxes = 5 × 16 = 80 kg; total of 4 = 4 × 15 = 60 kg; fifth = 20 kg — **follows**. II: the first four only average 15 kg; they could be 25, 15, 10 and 10 kg, and 25 kg is heavier than the fifth box — **does not follow**. Answer: **only I**.
practice.shortcut: New item = new total − old total. An average never fixes the largest value.

practice.q:
**Statement:** Only residents of the housing society can use its swimming pool. Meena is not a resident of the society.

**Conclusions:**
I. Meena cannot use the society's swimming pool.
II. Every resident of the society uses the swimming pool.

Which of the conclusions follow(s) from the statement?
practice.solution: 'Only residents' is a gate: anyone who is not a resident is out, so I **follows**. The gate says who *may* use the pool, not that every resident *does* — II **does not follow**. Answer: **only I**.
practice.shortcut: 'Only X' tells you who is out, never that every X does it.

practice.q:
**Statement:** Every customer who shops for more than ₹2,000 at a store gets a free cloth bag. Sunil got a free cloth bag from the store.

**Conclusions:**
I. Sunil shopped for more than ₹2,000.
II. A customer who shops for ₹2,500 at the store gets a free cloth bag.

Which of the conclusions follow(s) from the statement?
practice.solution: The rule says shopping above ₹2,000 is *enough* for a bag; it does not say it is the *only* way to get one, so from Sunil's bag we cannot work backwards — I **does not follow**. ₹2,500 is more than ₹2,000, so that customer is covered by 'every' — II **follows**. Answer: **only II**.
practice.shortcut: 'Every X gets Y' runs forward (X → Y), not backward (Y → X).

practice.q:
**Statement:** Water supply in Ward 5 will be stopped on Thursday from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. for repair of the pipeline.

**Conclusions:**
I. Residents of Ward 5 will not get piped water at 11 a.m. on Thursday.
II. The pipeline serving Ward 5 needs repair.

Which of the conclusions follow(s) from the statement?
practice.solution: 11 a.m. lies inside the 9 a.m.–1 p.m. shutdown — I **follows**. The shutdown is 'for repair of the pipeline', so II restates the stated reason — **follows**. Answer: **both**.
practice.shortcut: Restatements of the time window and the stated reason both follow.

practice.q:
**Statement:** From next month, the bank will stay open till 7 p.m. on weekdays instead of closing at 4 p.m.

**Conclusions:**
I. The bank will stay open three hours longer on weekdays.
II. The bank will also remain open on Sundays.
III. Customers will be able to visit the bank at 6 p.m. on a weekday next month.

Which of the conclusions follow(s) from the statement?
options: All of I, II and III follow
practice.solution: I: 4 p.m. to 7 p.m. is 3 hours — **follows**. II: only weekdays are mentioned — **does not follow**. III: 6 p.m. is within the new timing — **follows**. Answer: **only I and III**.
practice.shortcut: Tick each conclusion separately, then match the pair.

practice.q:
**Statement:** Out of the 60 employees of an office, 45 travel to work by metro.

**Conclusions:**
I. 75% of the employees travel to work by metro.
II. 15 employees travel to work by car.

Which of the conclusions follow(s) from the statement?
practice.solution: I: 45 ÷ 60 × 100 = 75% — **follows**. II: 15 employees do not use the metro, but they may walk, cycle or take a bus — 'by car' is not given — **does not follow**. Answer: **only I**.
practice.shortcut: The remainder is 'not metro', not any particular mode.

practice.q:
**Statement:** 'Drink only boiled water during the monsoon,' the doctor advised the villagers.

**Assumptions:**
I. Boiling can make water safer to drink.
II. The villagers are able to boil their drinking water.

Which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement?
options: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
practice.solution: Negate I: boiling does not make water safer — the advice becomes pointless, so I is **implicit**. Negate II: villagers cannot boil water — then the advice cannot be followed, so II is **implicit**. Answer: **both**.
practice.shortcut: Advice assumes it helps AND that the listener can follow it.

practice.q:
**Statement:** A father told his daughter, 'Leave home by 8 a.m., or you will miss the 9 a.m. bus.'

**Assumptions:**
I. The daughter needs to catch the 9 a.m. bus.
II. The bus stop is exactly one hour away from home.

Which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement?
options: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit
practice.solution: Negate I: she does not need that bus — the warning is pointless, so I is **implicit**. II fixes the travel time at 'exactly' one hour; the father only needs the journey to take enough time that leaving later is risky — II is **not implicit**. Answer: **only I**.
practice.shortcut: Words like 'exactly' make an assumption too precise to be needed.

practice.q:
**Statement:** 'Book your train tickets at least a month in advance for Diwali travel,' a travel agent told his customers.

**Assumptions:**
I. Tickets for Diwali travel may not be available closer to the date.
II. Train fares are lower when tickets are booked a month in advance.

Which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement?
options: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
practice.solution: Negate I: tickets will be easily available even later — booking early is pointless, so I is **implicit**. Negate II: fares are the same — the advice still makes sense because of availability, so II is **not implicit**. Answer: **only I**.
practice.shortcut: If the advice survives the negation, the assumption is not needed.

practice.q:
**Statement:** Advertisement: 'Fresh vegetables delivered to your door within 30 minutes — order on our app!'

**Assumptions:**
I. Some people want fresh vegetables delivered quickly.
II. Some people are able to place orders through a mobile app.

Which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement?
options: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit
practice.solution: Negate I: nobody wants quick delivery — the advert's hook is useless, so I is **implicit**. Negate II: nobody can order through an app — no one can respond, so II is **implicit**. Answer: **both**.
practice.shortcut: An advert assumes its hook attracts someone and that someone can respond.

practice.q:
**Statement:** Notice in a housing society: 'The overhead water tank will be cleaned on Sunday from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Residents are requested to store water in advance.'

**Assumptions:**
I. Residents will read the notice before Sunday.
II. Cleaning the tank will take a whole week.

Which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement?
options: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
practice.solution: Negate I: nobody reads it in time — the notice is useless, so I is **implicit**. II contradicts the notice, which gives a four-hour window — **not implicit**. Answer: **only I**.
practice.shortcut: An assumption that contradicts the statement can never be implicit.

practice.q:
**Statement:** Advertisement: 'Our water purifier removes 99% of germs. Buy one for your family's health.'

**Assumptions:**
I. All other water purifiers remove fewer germs than this one.
II. Some buyers are concerned about germs in their drinking water.

Which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement?
options: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
practice.solution: I compares the product with every rival; the advert makes no such claim and does not need it — **not implicit**. Negate II: no buyer cares about germs — the hook '99% of germs' is useless, so II is **implicit**. Answer: **only II**.
practice.shortcut: Adverts assume buyer interest, not superiority over all rivals.

practice.q:
**Statement:** The municipal corporation has decided to plant 10,000 trees along city roads to reduce air pollution.

**Assumptions:**
I. After the trees are planted, the city will become completely free of air pollution.
II. Trees can help reduce air pollution to some extent.

Which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement?
options: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
practice.solution: I expects a total result; the corporation only needs some reduction to make the plan worthwhile — **not implicit**. Negate II: trees do nothing for pollution — the decision is pointless, so II is **implicit**. Answer: **only II**.
practice.shortcut: 'Completely' = total effect = not implicit. 'To some extent' = implicit.

practice.q:
**Statement:** A school has started a daily 15-minute reading period to improve students' reading habits.

**Assumptions:**
I. Every student will become a regular reader within a month.
II. At present, some students do not have a good reading habit.

Which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement?
options: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit
practice.solution: I is a total, time-bound result that no school can assume — **not implicit**. Negate II: every student already reads well — there is nothing to improve and the new period loses its purpose, so II is **implicit**. Answer: **only II**.
practice.shortcut: A step meant 'to improve' something assumes there is room to improve.

practice.q:
**Statement:** The railway has decided to run a special train between Delhi and Patna during the Chhath festival.

**Assumptions:**
I. Many people will want to travel between Delhi and Patna during the festival.
II. The railway has enough coaches and staff to run one more train.

Which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement?
options: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit
practice.solution: Negate I: no extra travellers — the special train is pointless, so I is **implicit**. Negate II: the railway cannot run another train — the decision cannot be carried out, so II is **implicit**. Answer: **both**.
practice.shortcut: A decision assumes a need (demand) and feasibility (resources).

practice.q:
**Statement:** A bank has decided to install ATMs in 50 villages of a district.

**Assumptions:**
I. The bank will close all its branches in the district.
II. People in these villages are likely to use the ATMs.

Which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement?
options: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit
practice.solution: I is an unrelated extra step; opening ATMs does not require closing branches — **not implicit**. Negate II: nobody will use the ATMs — the decision is pointless, so II is **implicit**. Answer: **only II**.
practice.shortcut: Reject unrelated extra steps; keep the need behind the decision.

practice.q:
**Statement:** The government will give free cooking-gas connections to poor families to reduce smoke inside homes.

**Assumptions:**
I. Some poor families use fuels that produce smoke while cooking.
II. Every poor family will stop using firewood completely.

Which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement?
options: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit
practice.solution: Negate I: no poor family uses smoky fuel — the scheme has no purpose, so I is **implicit**. II expects a complete change by every family; some reduction is enough reason for the scheme — **not implicit**. Answer: **only I**.
practice.shortcut: Total words — every, completely — mark the trap.

practice.q:
**Statement:** Many streetlights in a colony have not been working for two weeks, and residents feel unsafe at night.

**Courses of action:**
I. The civic body should repair the streetlights at once.
II. Residents should be banned from going out after dark.

Which of the courses of action follow(s)?
options: Only course of action I follows
Only course of action II follows
practice.solution: I fixes the actual problem — **follows**. II restricts everyone instead of fixing the lights — impractical and unfair, **does not follow**. Answer: **only I**.
practice.shortcut: Fix the fault; do not ban the people.

practice.q:
**Statement:** A private bus operator was found charging passengers double the fixed fare on a route.

**Courses of action:**
I. All private buses in the state should be banned.
II. Action should be taken against the operator as per the rules.

Which of the courses of action follow(s)?
options: Only course of action I follows
Only course of action II follows
practice.solution: I punishes every operator in the state for one operator's fault — a blanket ban, **does not follow**. II targets the one who broke the rule — **follows**. Answer: **only II**.
practice.shortcut: One offender → act on that offender, not the whole sector.

practice.q:
**Statement:** Cracks have appeared in a bridge that was built only two years ago.

**Courses of action:**
I. Heavy vehicles should not be allowed on the bridge until engineers check it.
II. An inquiry should be held into the construction and action taken against those found responsible.
III. The state should stop building new bridges.

Which of the courses of action follow(s)?
options: All of I, II and III follow
practice.solution: I is an immediate safety step — **follows**. II finds the cause and fixes responsibility — **follows**. III is a sweeping reaction to one bridge's defect — **does not follow**. Answer: **only I and II**.
practice.shortcut: Safety now + inquiry follows; a blanket stop does not.

practice.q:
**Statement:** Dengue cases in the city have risen sharply this month.

**Courses of action:**
I. The civic body should clear stagnant water where mosquitoes breed.
II. Government hospitals should set up special fever counters.

Which of the courses of action follow(s)?
options: Only course of action II follows
Only course of action I follows
practice.solution: I attacks the cause (breeding sites) — **follows**. II gives relief to those already ill — **follows**. Prevention and relief do not cancel each other. Answer: **both**.
practice.shortcut: Prevention + relief can both follow.

practice.q:
**Statement:** Heavy rain has flooded the low-lying areas of a town and many families are stranded.

**Courses of action:**
I. Rescue teams with boats should be sent to the flooded areas.
II. Drainage in these areas should be improved before the next monsoon.

Which of the courses of action follow(s)?
options: Only course of action II follows
Only course of action I follows
practice.solution: I is urgent relief for stranded families — **follows**. II prevents a repeat — **follows**. One is short-term, the other long-term; both are sensible. Answer: **both**.
practice.shortcut: Do not reject relief for being temporary or a fix for being slow.

practice.q:
**Statement:** The reservoir that supplies water to a city has fallen to a very low level after poor rainfall.

**Courses of action:**
I. Water should be rationed and residents urged to use it carefully.
II. Tankers should be sent to areas facing an acute shortage.
III. The city's population should be shifted to another city.

Which of the courses of action follow(s)?
options: All of I, II and III follow
practice.solution: I stretches the available water — **follows**. II gives relief where it is worst — **follows**. III is absurd and impractical — **does not follow**. Answer: **only I and II**.
practice.shortcut: Reject only the absurd option; relief steps can all follow.

practice.q:
**Statement:** Passengers are missing trains because the display boards at a station often show wrong platform numbers.

**Courses of action:**
I. The display system should be checked and corrected.
II. Ticket prices of all trains should be reduced.

Which of the courses of action follow(s)?
options: Only course of action I follows
Only course of action II follows
practice.solution: I fixes the exact cause of the problem — **follows**. II has nothing to do with wrong platform numbers — **does not follow**. Answer: **only I**.
practice.shortcut: Name the problem; keep only actions that touch it.

practice.q:
**Statement:** For three years, the Class X mathematics results of a village school have been very poor.

**Courses of action:**
I. The road to the village should be widened.
II. A qualified mathematics teacher should be appointed and extra classes arranged.

Which of the courses of action follow(s)?
options: Only course of action I follows
Only course of action II follows
practice.solution: I may be useful in general but does not address poor maths results — **does not follow**. II directly targets the weak subject — **follows**. Answer: **only II**.
practice.shortcut: A good-sounding action on a different problem does not follow.

practice.q:
**Statement:** A few students of a college were caught copying in the final examination.

**Courses of action:**
I. The results of all students of the college should be cancelled.
II. Action should be taken against those caught and invigilation should be made stricter.

Which of the courses of action follow(s)?
options: Only course of action I follows
Only course of action II follows
practice.solution: I punishes honest students for the fault of a few — **does not follow**. II acts on the wrongdoers and prevents a repeat — **follows**. Answer: **only II**.
practice.shortcut: Act against the few who did wrong, not against everyone.

practice.q:
**Statement:** Some shopkeepers in a market were found selling adulterated milk.

**Courses of action:**
I. Milk samples from shops in the market should be tested and those found guilty punished.
II. All milk shops in the city should be closed permanently.

Which of the courses of action follow(s)?
options: Only course of action II follows
Only course of action I follows
practice.solution: I identifies and punishes the actual offenders — **follows**. II shuts every honest shop in the whole city for ever — disproportionate, **does not follow**. Answer: **only I**.
practice.shortcut: Test, trace, punish the guilty — never shut everything.

practice.q:
**Statement:** Every summer, many people in a town fall ill due to heatstroke.

**Courses of action:**
I. All offices in the town should be closed for the entire summer.
II. A new cricket stadium should be built in the town.

Which of the courses of action follow(s)?
options: Only course of action I follows
Only course of action II follows
practice.solution: I is impractical — a town cannot stop all work for months — **does not follow**. II is unrelated to heatstroke — **does not follow**. Useful steps would be awareness drives, drinking-water points or treatment facilities. Answer: **neither**.
practice.shortcut: When both options are extreme or unrelated, 'neither' is the answer.
